# Paper summaries — the 12 new papers (folders 731–742)

Each entry: what the paper does, then **For kfault** — the specific hook into
your argument. Numbers are taken from the papers' own abstracts.

## §2.3 Weak oracles and test inadequacy

### [731] EvalPlus — Liu, Xia, Wang & Zhang, NeurIPS 2023
*Is Your Code Generated by ChatGPT Really Correct?* — arXiv 2305.01210

The authors argue that code benchmarks are limited by the quantity and quality of their test cases, so a program can pass and still be wrong. They build EvalPlus, a framework that augments an existing benchmark with automatically generated test inputs (LLM-based and mutation-based), and apply it to HumanEval to produce HumanEval+, extending the test cases by **80×**. Evaluating 26 LLMs including GPT-4 and ChatGPT, the added tests catch large amounts of previously undetected wrong code and reduce pass@k by **19.3–28.9%**. They also find that test insufficiency causes **mis-ranking**: WizardCoder-CodeLlama and Phind-CodeLlama beat ChatGPT on HumanEval+ but not on HumanEval.

**For kfault.** This is your method's precedent and your most important missing citation. It establishes that (a) adding tests to an existing benchmark is accepted practice, not an invented penalty, and (b) the effect size you found is normal, not suspicious. The mis-ranking result is the strongest hook: your false-pass rates differ by model (GLM-5 14%, DeepSeek 16%, Qwen 7% one-shot), so **KernelBench may mis-rank kernel-generating models the same way** — a claim you can make directly from your own data and attribute the mechanism to Liu et al. Your extension beyond EvalPlus is the repair dimension: they measure a static benchmark once, you measure how the gap *moves across repair turns*.

### [733] Kaizen — Ludwig et al., 2026
*Metamorphic Fuzzing and Differential Testing for LLM-Translated HPC Applications* — arXiv 2607.04058

Kaizen evaluates the correctness of LLM-translated HPC code (CUDA→OpenMP) using three techniques: metamorphic fuzzing via source mutation to create semantically equivalent programs, grammar-based input fuzzing for behavioural diversity, and differential testing against the original. Evaluated on 16 scientific applications across seven domains with three fine-tuned LLMs, at kernel and full-program granularity. Findings: compilation success is a poor proxy for correctness; translated programs show systematic compile-error patterns (9 categories at kernel level, 27 at full-program level); **semantic errors that survive compilation are often input-dependent and require differential testing to expose**; full-program translation is much harder than kernel-level.

**For kfault.** The closest methodological sibling you have, and it arrived after your proposal. "Semantic errors that compile and pass developer-written tests yet produce incorrect scientific results" is your `silent` category in different words, and "input-dependent" is exactly why your non-contiguous probe works. Use it two ways: as **independent confirmation** that the phenomenon is real outside your setup, and as a **scope contrast** — Kaizen studies *translation* between programming models with no repair loop; you study *generation* plus repair, and you measure the false-pass rate rather than cataloguing error types. Cite it in your limitations too: it validates against a reference implementation the same way you validate against PyTorch.

### [738] Segura, Fraser, Sanchez & Ruiz-Cortés — IEEE TSE 42(9), 2016
*A Survey on Metamorphic Testing* — DOI 10.1109/TSE.2016.2532875

A survey of metamorphic testing, a technique for the **oracle problem**: when you cannot predict the correct output for a given input, you instead define a *metamorphic relation* — a transformation of the input and the corresponding expected change (or non-change) in the output. Introduced in 1998, applied across domains from web services to computer graphics. The survey covers results, application areas, empirical practice and open challenges.

**For kfault.** This gives your stress battery a name and a 25-year pedigree. Your probes are metamorphic relations: *"making the input non-contiguous must not change the output"*, *"repeating the input must produce the repeated output"*. Framing them this way does real defensive work on your weakest point — 85% of your silent failures come from the non-contiguous probe alone, and a reviewer could call that an arbitrary penalty. Under a metamorphic framing it is a standard, well-motivated relation for a drop-in replacement, and the burden shifts to whoever wants to argue that layout-dependence is acceptable in a PyTorch operator.

### [739] Dixit et al., Facebook, 2021
*Silent Data Corruptions at Scale* — arXiv 2102.11245

Describes Silent Data Corruption (SDC) in Facebook's production fleet: computational errors not caught by CPU error-reporting, invisible at the hardware level, that propagate up the stack and surface as application-level problems, sometimes costing months of debugging. The paper covers manufacturing defect types, a real datacenter case study with the root-cause and triage flow, and mitigations. Across hundreds of thousands of machines monitored for over 18 months, hundreds of CPUs were found to exhibit these errors — a systemic issue across processor generations.

**For kfault.** One sentence of framing, but a valuable one. It licenses your vocabulary: *silent* is an established term in systems and fault tolerance for "wrong result, no error signal", and your repo is called kfault. Use it in your introduction to argue that silent failures are treated as a first-class reliability concern elsewhere in computing, and that LLM kernel generation currently has no equivalent notion. Pair it with the observation that a silent kernel is *worse* than a mercurial core, because it is deterministic and will be shipped.

### [741] Hochschild et al., Google, HotOS 2021
*Cores That Don't Count* — DOI 10.1145/3458336.3465297

Argues that the industry's assumption of fail-stop processors is a fiction. As feature sizes shrink and specialised instruction-silicon pairings proliferate, Google observes ephemeral computational errors that manufacturing tests did not catch, cannot always be fixed by microcode, and are often correlated with specific components. They call such a core **"mercurial."** These failures are typically *silent* — the only symptom is an erroneous computation. The paper is a call to action for detection, isolation and tolerance mechanisms.

**For kfault.** Interchangeable with [739]; pick one. This one has the better opening line for a dissertation introduction — *"imagine you are running a massive-scale data-analysis pipeline in production, and one day it starts to give you wrong answers"* — and "the only symptom is an erroneous computation" is a quotable definition of your `silent` category. Keep it to a sentence or two; this is framing, not evidence.

## §2.4 Iterative repair and self-correction

### [735] Chen, Lin, Schärli & Zhou — 2023
*Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug* — arXiv 2304.05128

Proposes SELF-DEBUGGING, teaching a model to debug its own predicted program through few-shot demonstrations. The model performs "rubber duck debugging": without human feedback on correctness, it identifies mistakes by inspecting execution results and explaining its own code in natural language. On Spider (text-to-SQL, no unit tests available) it improves the baseline by **2–3%**, and by **9%** on the hardest problems; on TransCoder and MBPP, where unit tests exist, by up to **12%**. By reusing failed predictions it also improves sample efficiency, matching or beating baselines that generate 10× more candidates.

**For kfault.** The canonical citation for the repair loop your pipeline implements — cite it when you introduce your multi-turn design, so the loop is recognisably the standard pattern rather than something you invented. Two details matter for your argument. First, its gains are measured *entirely* by benchmark pass rate, with no check on whether repaired programs are correct beyond the tests — the blind spot your dissertation quantifies. Second, its gains are larger where unit tests are available, which makes the quality of the feedback signal the active ingredient; your stage-4 withholding is a deliberate manipulation of exactly that ingredient.

### [736] Madaan et al., NeurIPS 2023
*Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback* — arXiv 2303.17651

Introduces SELF-REFINE: an LLM generates an initial output, then the *same* model provides feedback on it and refines it, iteratively. No supervised training data, no extra training, no reinforcement learning — one model acting as generator, refiner and feedback provider. Evaluated on 7 tasks with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, outputs are preferred by humans and automatic metrics over conventional one-step generation, improving task performance by roughly **20% absolute on average**.

**For kfault.** The origin of the "just iterate" pattern that every agentic CUDA system now inherits, and the source of the ~20% headline improvements that made repair loops standard. Cite it as the optimistic thesis your finding qualifies: refinement does improve the measured score — your data agrees, pass rates rise substantially — but the metric doing the measuring has to be trusted for that improvement to mean what it appears to mean. Note also that Self-Refine's feedback is *self*-generated, whereas your repair loop receives real execution feedback, so your setup is the more favourable case and the relocation effect still appears.

### [740] Shinn et al., 2023
*Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning* — arXiv 2303.11366

Proposes Reflexion, which reinforces language agents through linguistic feedback rather than weight updates. Agents verbally reflect on task feedback signals and store these reflections in an episodic memory buffer to improve decisions on later trials. It handles scalar or free-form feedback from external or internally simulated sources, and improves over baselines on sequential decision-making, coding and language reasoning — notably **91% pass@1 on HumanEval, versus 80% for the previous state-of-the-art GPT-4**.

**For kfault.** Optional; [736] covers the same ground. Its value is that the HumanEval number (91% vs 80%) is one of the most-cited results driving adoption of repair loops — and HumanEval is precisely the benchmark that EvalPlus [731] showed over-reports correctness by up to 28.9%. If you want one sharp sentence connecting §2.3 to §2.4, it is that the flagship self-correction result was measured on a benchmark independently shown to be too weak to detect wrong code. Do not overstate it — EvalPlus does not evaluate Reflexion specifically — but the tension is real and worth a line.

### [732] Olausson, Inala, Wang, Gao & Solar-Lezama — ICLR 2024
*Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?* — arXiv 2306.09896

A critical study of self-repair with Code Llama, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on HumanEval and APPS. When the **cost** of repair is accounted for — repair needs extra model calls, so the fair baseline is drawing more i.i.d. samples at equal compute — the gains are often modest, vary widely across data subsets, and are sometimes absent entirely. The authors hypothesise that self-repair is **bottlenecked by the model's ability to give feedback on its own code**; artificially boosting feedback quality with a stronger model produces substantially larger gains, and human feedback larger still.

**For kfault.** Your closest ally and the paper your gap statement should build on. They establish that repair's benefits are **overstated on the efficiency axis**; you extend the critique to a new axis they did not examine — repair's benefits are also overstated on the **trustworthiness** axis, because some of the recorded successes are failures the benchmark can no longer see. Their feedback-bottleneck hypothesis also supplies your mechanism: your repair loop feeds back loud errors (compile messages, crashes, `allclose` mismatches) and nothing about layout or edge cases, so the model optimises against exactly the signal it receives. That is why a `runtime` failure becomes `silent` rather than `pass` — the observed shape in 40 of your chains. Cite Olausson at the moment you explain the mechanism, not just in related work.

### [734] Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song & Zhou — ICLR 2024
*Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet* — arXiv 2310.01798

Examines **intrinsic self-correction**: a model correcting its initial response using only its own capabilities, with no external feedback. The finding is that LLMs struggle in this setting and performance frequently **degrades** after self-correction. Critically, the authors show that reported improvements in earlier work (e.g. Kim et al., Shinn et al.) came from using **oracle labels** to guide the process, and those improvements **vanish when oracle labels are unavailable**. They also argue self-correction must be compared against baselines at equivalent inference cost.

**For kfault.** This is the paper that justifies your single most important design decision. Your stage 4 is **withheld** from the repair prompt precisely so the model cannot use it as an oracle — and Huang et al. give you the citation showing why that matters: when a held-out signal leaks into the loop, apparent improvement is the model fitting the oracle, not getting better. Without this citation, "we withheld stage 4" reads as an arbitrary choice; with it, it is the methodologically required one, and an examiner asking *"why not just feed the stress results back?"* has a published answer. The equivalent-inference-cost point also strengthens your limitations section: your 4-turn arms should ideally be compared against 4 independent samples, which is a clean piece of further work to propose.

### [742] Wei et al., NeurIPS 2022
*Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models* — arXiv 2201.11903

Shows that prompting a model to generate a chain of intermediate reasoning steps substantially improves complex reasoning, and that this ability emerges in sufficiently large models. With eight chain-of-thought exemplars, PaLM 540B reaches state-of-the-art on GSM8K, beating a finetuned GPT-3 with a verifier. Gains hold across arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning.

**For kfault.** Background for your think/direct arms — one or two sentences. Worth noting that your design is stronger than prompt-level CoT: you toggle `reasoning_effort` on **identical weights**, so the comparison is not confounded by different checkpoints or prompts. Cite Wei to define the mechanism, then state that distinction explicitly, because it is a genuine methodological advantage over the proposal's original R1-vs-V3 plan and should not pass unremarked.

## §2.2 Kernel benchmarks

### [737] Zhu et al., 2026
*CUDABench: Benchmarking LLMs for Text-to-CUDA Generation* — arXiv 2603.02236

Argues that existing kernel benchmarks focus on translating high-level code (e.g. PyTorch) into CUDA — a **code-to-code translation** regime where structure and computational intent are already specified — and therefore miss the harder **text-to-CUDA** setting, where the model must infer algorithmic intent from natural language across domains beyond ML at production input scales. CUDABench provides a Breadth-Depth-Difficulty task set spanning AI, scientific computing and data analytics, plus a scoring pipeline covering compilation correctness, functional consistency via execution-based verification, and a roofline-based Performance-Score. Headline finding: a **notable mismatch between high compilation success rates and low functional correctness**, along with weak domain-specific algorithmic knowledge and poor GPU resource utilisation.

**For kfault.** Two jobs. First, it is the direct source for the reasoning-vs-correctness split your proposal §3.3 asserts — the compile/correctness mismatch is stated in its abstract, so cite it there rather than leaning only on Ouyang. Second, it gives you a clean scope sentence: CUDABench classifies KernelBench as code-to-code translation and moves *sideways* to a harder input format, whereas your work stays in KernelBench's setting and moves *downwards*, asking whether the correctness check at the bottom of the pipeline is sound. Different axis, no overlap — say so in one line and the reviewer stops wondering.

## How these change your chapter

1. **§2.3 now exists.** EvalPlus + Segura + Kaizen turn your stress battery from an invention into an instance of established practice. This is the single biggest improvement to the review.
2. **Your mechanism has citations.** Olausson's feedback bottleneck explains *why* repair relocates failures; Huang's oracle-label result justifies withholding stage 4. Both belong in the design chapter, not only in related work.
3. **A new claim, now verified against your data** (`misranking.py`, run 9 Aug 2026). EvalPlus's mis-ranking effect is present, and it is *caused by repair*:

   | think arm | strict rank | extended rank |
   |---|---|---|
   | one-shot (turn 0) | Qwen > GLM-5 > DeepSeek | Qwen > GLM-5 > DeepSeek |
   | after 3 repair turns | GLM-5 > DeepSeek > **Qwen** | **Qwen** > GLM-5 > DeepSeek |

   At turn 0 both definitions agree. After repair the strict ranking **inverts** — Qwen falls from first to last — while the extended ranking is unchanged. Under the strict contract the three models converge to 91.5% / 92.5% / 93.5%, a statistical tie (McNemar, all pairwise *p* > 0.52). Under the extended contract Qwen leads by 8 points (*p* = 0.037 pooled; *p* = 0.12–0.23 per device, same direction on both GPUs).

   So repair does not only inflate scores, it **destroys the benchmark's ability to tell the models apart**. Cite Liu et al. for the mechanism, and note that they observed mis-ranking in a static benchmark whereas here it is *induced* by the repair loop — a stronger version of their effect that no prior work reports. Not present in the `direct` arm, where models are far from the ceiling.
